strengths: Novel problem formulation and first systematic study of reference-based temporal effect transfer in videos, addressing a natural gap in existing work

Substantial dataset contribution: 120K+ triplets covering 1,700+ effects from three complementary sources (LoRA I2V, scalable V2V pipeline, code-based effects). The V2V pipeline is clever and scalable engineering
Comprehensive and convincing human evaluation with 1,000+ annotations showing strong win rates (78-98% for V2V, 75-82% for I2V, 94-98% for code-based) with consistent positive score deltas
Strong generalization to unseen effects: testing on held-out LoRA effects and novel prompts demonstrates transfer of temporal dynamics independent of specific effect instances
Clear presentation with well-designed figures, detailed supplementary materials, explicit limitation discussion, and reproducibility focus (promised code/dataset release)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution is straightforward extension of Wan conditioning to handle two inputs via latent concatenation. No novel diffusion mechanisms, attention designs, or disentanglement strategies proposed

Quantitative metrics partially contradict claims: first-frame similarity favors baselines (Table 3: 0.7698 vs 0.7799), and input preservation is weaker than depth-conditioned VACE (Table 4: 0.8568 vs 0.9460), suggesting input fidelity tradeoffs not fully addressed
Significant practical limitations: inference time doubled (~7 min vs 3.5 min), limiting deployment scalability. Unclear if training converged or method is compute-inefficient
Insufficient ablations: no isolation of data source contributions (LoRA vs V2V vs code), no conditioning mechanism comparisons, cannot assess dataset-size vs method-innovation contribution

Dataset composition bias and domain limitations: heavy focus on human-centric scenes, LoRA-based effects inherit upstream model biases, code-based effects are synthetic creating distribution gap. Generalization to environments and abstract effects unclear
Evaluation relies on surrogate metrics without ground truth triplets. User study uses binary ratings rather than continuous scores. Limited failure mode analysis beyond occlusion struggles

Unclear generalization: model trained on specific effect families (LoRA, V2V, code-based). Testing on held-out prompts within same families is weaker than truly novel effects. No evaluation on professional or user-created effects
Architecture lacks mathematical rigor: Figure 5 shows approach but design choices (width-wise vs channel-wise concatenation) lack justification. Conditioning mechanism details missing

weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Model architecture is a straightforward concatenation of existing Wan components; conditioning mechanism uses standard latent concatenation without methodological innovation

Severe reproducibility concerns: Code unavailable until publication; dataset presumably proprietary; heavy reliance on external proprietary models (Wan, Qwen, Flux) creates dependency and non-reproducibility

Synthetic data cascade problems: V2V pipeline uses image generation/editing models introducing compound errors and domain shift; no quality control metrics reported; no ground truth validation possible
Circular dataset construction: Effects are engineered to be transferrable within the framework; unclear generalization to real-world effect specifications

Fundamental limitations inadequately addressed: Computational cost (~7 min/video, 2× baseline) contradicts 'practical' claims; generalization limited to similar LoRA/operation families; domain bias toward human-centric scenes acknowledged but unresolved

strengths: Addresses a novel and practical problem—transferring temporal video effects via reference conditioning—which is more expressive than text-only or keyframe-conditioned approaches
Large-scale, high-quality dataset of 120K+ triplets covering 1,700+ effects from three complementary sources; the scalable video-to-video generation pipeline is innovative and reusable
Comprehensive human evaluation with 15,000+ annotations from 500+ annotators using rigorous methodology (bootstrap resampling, multi-criteria evaluation, quality-controlled HITs)
Consistent empirical improvements over strong baselines across multiple evaluation criteria, with proper generalization testing (unseen LoRAs, novel prompts)
Thoughtful dataset construction combining LoRA-based effects, custom V2V pipeline, and code-based effects to maximize diversity
Strong technical soundness: triplet construction, training procedure, and evaluation methodology are well-designed and properly motivated
Excellent reproducibility support: detailed implementation details, code to be released, comprehensive dataset documentation
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: model is straightforward extension of Wan2.1 using width-wise latent concatenation; no novel conditioning mechanisms or diffusion innovations

Entirely synthetic video-to-video dataset: all V2V training pairs are generated, not recorded, creating potential distribution shift; validation set is also synthetic with no ground-truth triplets for assessment

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing temporal effect transfer, a genuine gap in video editing literature
Comprehensive dataset construction with a scalable V2V generation pipeline combining three complementary data sources (LoRA-based, neural V2V, code-based effects)
Rigorous human evaluation methodology with 15,000+ annotations from 500+ annotators and proper statistical validation (bootstrap confidence intervals)
Practical feed-forward inference without test-time optimization or per-effect tuning
Honest discussion of limitations including occlusions, human-centric dataset bias, and computational costs
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the architecture is a straightforward extension of Wan2.1 with basic channel concatenation for conditioning. No significant algorithmic innovation beyond combining existing techniques.

Critical absence of ablation studies makes it impossible to assess individual component contributions. Missing ablations: dataset source impacts, reference conditioning benefit vs. text-only, architectural design choices, whether temporal dynamics are learned.

Weak baseline comparisons: all baselines are prompt-only methods not designed for reference-based effects, creating an unfair comparison. User study win margins are modest (57-62% in V2V, 56.8-57.4% in I2V), barely above chance level.

Dataset quality concerns inadequately addressed: V2V pipeline relies on cascading AI models with unquantified error propagation; manual filtering details absent (% filtered, quality metrics); heavy reliance on synthetic data with unclear real-world generalization.

Validation set design bias: V2V validation uses 'novel prompts' but identical generation pipeline as training, keeping validation within training distribution. Claims of generalization to unseen categories are overstated—only permutations, not fundamentally new effect types.

Quantitative metrics acknowledged as inadequate but unresolved. Tables 3-4 show our method has lower first-frame similarity than baselines (0.7698 vs 0.7911), suggesting potential under-editing. Indirect metric proxies (VideoPrism embedding similarity) poorly capture effect transfer quality.

Reproducibility barriers: code and dataset remain unreleased with only promises of future release; heavy dependence on proprietary models (Wan2.1, Qwen); sparse architectural details in appendix; triplet construction logic not thoroughly validated.

Insufficient mechanistic analysis: no investigation of what features enable effect transfer, minimal failure case analysis (one example in Figure 9), no effect-category breakdown, absent sensitivity analyses for guidance scales/prompt quality.

Methodological gaps: text dependency in V2V effects not analyzed; first-last frame conditioning assumption unclear for non-linear effects; guidance normalization (Eq. 1) is ad-hoc and unjustified; 2x computational cost dismissed despite severe practical implications.
Paper framing mismatch: reads as a dataset/application paper but positioned as a methods contribution. Technical contribution insufficient for a methods-focused venue if dataset/code not public.
